sections.h2: Looking up Volusia County property records online
sections.html:
Two county sites answer most questions. The clerk's Official Records inquiry returns the index and images of recorded papers dating from April 4, 1988: deeds, mortgages, judgments, marriages, divorces, powers of attorney and probate items. A paper appears only after it has been recorded, indexed, verified and released, so a filing from the last few days may not show yet.

The Property Appraiser's search menu is broader. Choose real property by name, address or alternate key, an advanced search by fields and ranges, personal property, sales, or an interactive map. Real property results export to CSV or a mailing list. Put simply, the clerk shows what was recorded against a parcel, and the appraiser shows what the parcel is, who the roll lists as owner and what has sold nearby.

sections.h2: Clerk charges to record a deed
sections.html:
The first page of an instrument no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches costs $10.00, with $8.50 for every page after that. Names past the fourth cost $1.00 apiece to index. State deed tax comes on top, at 70 cents per $100 of consideration or fraction of it.

Deed recording charges, Volusia County clerk

No mortgage balance comes off the consideration before the tax is figured, and a token recital like ten dollars and other valuable consideration still triggers the minimum tax. Each party to the deed answers for the tax, regardless of who agreed to pay it.

sections.h2: What a deed needs before the clerk will accept it
sections.html:
Bring the signed original, since photocopies are refused. The deed checklist sets out the layout and content.

  • Leave a 3 by 3 inch blank box in the upper right corner for the office stamp.
  • Write out the legal description and add the parcel ID number.
  • Print every signer's name under the signature along with a mailing address.
  • Show the grantee's name and mailing address (a mortgage is the exception).
  • Print the preparer's name and address.
  • Have two witnesses sign, each with a printed name and address.
  • Attach a notary certificate that satisfies Florida notary rules.

Florida's conveyance statute also calls for two subscribing witnesses and permits witnessing over audio-video technology. Other statutes can affect a given transfer, so an owner with an odd situation should see an attorney. Make the check payable to the Clerk of the Circuit Court.

Four routes are open: walk in at DeLand, use the Daytona Beach drop box, mail it, or e-record through a vendor. The Recording Department is at the courthouse, Room A121, 101 N. Alabama Avenue, DeLand, where papers are recorded and returned while you wait. Questions go to 386-736-5912.

  • Daytona Beach: a drop box at the entrance of the Courthouse Annex, 125 East Orange Avenue. Staff collect at 7:00 a.m. each business day, with no same-day promise. Include a cover sheet, the original and payment.
  • By mail: Attention Recording Department, P.O. Box 6043, DeLand, FL 32721, with a stamped return envelope. Acceptable payment is a check, money order, business check or cashier's check.
  • E-recording: Simplifile, CSC, ePN and Hopdox are the vendors, and the method is quicker and cheaper than paper.

sections.h2: Checking a parcel and nearby sales
sections.html:
Open the appraiser's real property search, enter a name, address or alternate key, then click through to the parcel record. The sales search filters by fields and ranges, which helps you see what nearby homes sold for before you set a price. The map search overlays parcel detail on a county map.

Exemption questions also go to the appraiser, with March 1 as the state filing deadline. After a sale, the following January 1 assessment follows the new owner at a reset value, so a buyer should not assume your bill carries over.

sections.h2: Foreclosure, tax deed and probate lists
sections.html:
Several clerk pages track property events. Weekly reports list new foreclosure suits in circuit and county courts and stay up for about 30 days. A daily list covers newly filed civil suits on the same 30 day basis. Tax deed information shows parcels headed to the next courthouse auction, and a Lands Available for Taxes list shows land that drew no bidders. A monthly probate report requires a subscriber login.

On a judicial foreclosure, the fee is $70.00 for conducting the sale and issuing and recording the title. State law puts the sale 20 to 35 days after judgment unless the plaintiff agrees to wait longer, the top bidder posts 5 percent, and objections are due within 10 days. A homeowner expecting surplus money should contact the clerk inside that same 10 day period.

Owners who end up in a property dispute meet a short list of clerk charges. An eviction seeking possession only costs $185.00, and so does one that adds damages up to $50,000. Summons issuance runs $10.00 per summons, with $2.50 more for each defendant past five. Garnishments and writs of attachment, replevin or distress are $85.00, and mediation is $60.00 per person.

  • Small claims filing fees climb by claim size, from $55.00 under $100 to $400.00 for claims from $15,001 to $50,000.
  • A judicial foreclosure sale fee of $70.00 covers conducting the sale and issuing and recording the title.
  • Timeshare foreclosures add $10.00 per unit above one, up to 15 units.

Charges change, so call the clerk's office before you file or pay. A records search costs $2.00 per year searched, and public records assistance is billed by the hour. Two courthouse locations serve the county: DeLand for recording and the Daytona Beach Courthouse Annex for a drop box.

sections.h2: What to verify before a sale closes
sections.html:
Look for open mortgages, liens and judgments in the Official Records and trace the chain of title. Match the legal description and parcel number against the appraiser's file, and fix any gap before you sign. Scan the foreclosure and tax deed pages too.

None of those reports replaces a title search, though they show whether a case has been filed against a parcel or an estate. If you inherited the house, probate filings are among the indexed official records. For past-due taxes or liens, request a payoff from the Volusia County tax collector, and ask your closing agent to confirm it before you accept any offer.

Once the checks are done, closing is simple. You sign the deed before two witnesses and a notary, the title company delivers it to the clerk with the fee and tax, and the recorded copy follows. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but the same record checks and payoffs still apply, so start them as soon as you decide to sell.

faqs.q: What does Volusia County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: Ten dollars for page one and $8.50 for each additional page, plus $1.00 per name beyond four. The 70 cent per $100 deed tax is charged in addition.

faqs.q: How old are the records in the Volusia County online index?
faqs.a: They start April 4, 1988 and run to the present. Only released items show, so brand-new filings can lag.

faqs.q: Will the Volusia County clerk take a deed by mail?
faqs.a: Yes, if you send the original with payment and a stamped return envelope to P.O. Box 6043, DeLand, FL 32721, marked for the Recording Department.

faqs.q: Is e-recording available in Volusia County?
faqs.a: Yes, through Simplifile, Corporate Service Company, eRecording Partners Network and Hopdox. It is faster and cheaper than paper.

faqs.q: How many people must witness a Volusia County deed?
faqs.a: Two, with printed names and addresses under their signatures. The Recording Department at 386-736-5912 can answer questions about unusual documents.
